{{Distinguish|circular sector}}
[[File:Ellipso-KSE0.svg|thumb|tri-axial ellipsoid with a circular section]]
In geometry, a '''circular section''' is a [[circle]] on a [[quadric]] surface (such as an [[ellipsoid]] or [[hyperboloid]]). It is a special [[plane (geometry)|plane]] section of the quadric, as this circle is the intersection with the quadric of the plane containing the circle.

Any plane section of a sphere is a circular section, if it contains at least 2 points. Any [[surface of revolution|quadric of revolution]] contains circles as sections with planes that are orthogonal to its axis; it does not contain any other circles, if it is not a sphere. More hidden are circles on other quadrics, such as tri-axial ellipsoids, elliptic cylinders, etc. Nevertheless, it is true that:
*Any quadric surface which contains ellipses contains circles, too.
Equivalently, all quadric surfaces contain circles except parabolic and hyperbolic [[cylinder]]s and hyperbolic [[paraboloid]]s.

If a quadric contains a circle, then every intersection of the quadric with a plane parallel to this circle is also a circle, provided it contains at least two points. Except for spheres, the circles contained in a quadric, if any, are all parallel to one of two fixed planes (which are equal in the case of a quadric of revolution).

Circular sections are used in [[crystallography]].<ref>W. H. Westphal: ''Physikalisches Wörterbuch: Zwei Teile in Einem Band.'' Springer-Verlag, 1952, {{ISBN|978-3-662-12707-0}}, p.&nbsp;350.</ref><ref>H. Tertsch: ''Die Festigkeitserscheinungen der Kristalle.'' Springer-Verlag, Wien, 1949, {{ISBN|978-3-211-80120-8}}, p.&nbsp;87.</ref><ref>G. Masing: ''Lehrbuch der Allgemeinen Metallkunde.'' Springer-Verlag, Berlin, 1950, {{ISBN|978-3-642-52-993-1}}, p.&nbsp;355.</ref>

==Using projective geometry==
The circular sections of a quadric may be computed from the [[implicit equation]] of the quadric, as it is done in the following sections. They may also be characterised and studied by using [[synthetic geometry|synthetic]] [[projective geometry]].

Let {{math|''C''}} be the intersection of a quadric surface {{math|''Q''}} and a plane {{math|''P''}}. In this section, {{math|''Q''}} and {{math|''C''}} are surfaces in the three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], which are extended to the [[projective space]] over the [[complex number]]s. Under these hypotheses, the curve {{math|''C''}} is a circle [[if and only if]] its intersection with the [[plane at infinity]] is included in the [[Glossary of classical algebraic geometry#O|ombilic]] (the curve at infinity of equation <math>x^2+y^2+z^2=0</math>).

The first case to be considered is when the intersection of {{math|''Q''}} with the plane at infinity consists of one or two real lines, that is when {{math|''Q''}} is either a [[hyperbolic paraboloid]], a [[parabolic cylinder]] or a [[cylinder#hyperbolic cylinder|hyperbolic cylinder]]. In this case the points at infinity of {{math|''C''}} are real (intersection of a real plane with real lines). Thus the plane sections of {{math|''Q''}} cannot be circles (neither [[ellipse]]s).

If {{math|''Q''}} is a [[sphere]], its intersection with the plane at infinity is the ombilic, and all plane sections are circles.

If {{math|''Q''}} is a [[surface of revolution]], its intersection with the ombilic consists of a pair of [[complex conjugate]] points (which are [[double point]]s). A real plane contains these two points if and only if it is perpendicular to the axis of revolution. Thus the circular sections are the plane sections by a plane perpendicular to the axis, that have at least two real points.

In the other cases, the intersection of {{math|''Q''}} with the ombilic consists of two different pairs of complex conjugate points. As {{math|''C''}} is a curve of degree two, its intersection with the plane at infinity consists of two points, possibly equal. The curve {{math|''C''}} is thus a circle, if these two points are one of these two pairs of complex conjugate points on the ombilic. Each of these pairs defines a [[Number line|real line]] (passing through the points), which is the intersection of {{math|''P''}} with the plane at infinity. Thus, one has a circular section if and only {{math|''C''}} has at least two real points and {{math|''P''}} contains one of these lines at infinity (that is if {{math|''P''}} is parallel to one of two directions defined by these lines at infinity).

== Determination of circular sections of a quadric ==
In order to find the planes, which contain circular sections of a given quadric, one uses the following statements:
:'''(S:)''' If the common points of a quadric with a ''sphere'' are contained in a pair of planes, then the intersection curve consists of two circles.
:'''(P:)''' If the intersection  of a plane and a quadric is a circle, then any parallel plane, that contains at least two points of the quadric, intersects the quadric in a circle, too.

Hence the ''strategy'' for the detection of circular sections is: 
:1) Find a ''sphere'' that intersects the quadric in a pair of planes and 
:2) The ''planes'' that are parallel to the detected ones deliver the remaining circular sections.

== Tri-axial ellipsoid ==
[[File:Ellipso-KSE.svg|thumb|upright=1.25|tri-axial ellipsoid with circular sections (blue and green) and the auxiliary sphere (red), which intersects the quadric in the blue circles]]
[[File:Ellipsoid-KSE-4-5.svg|thumb|Ellipsoid intersected by spheres: <math>c<{\color{seagreen}r_1}<{\color{blue}b}<{\color{purple}r_2}<a</math>]]
For the ellipsoid with equation 
:<math>\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}+\frac{z^2}{c^2}=1</math>
and the semi-axes  <math>a>b>c>0</math> one uses an auxiliary sphere with equation 
:<math>x^2+y^2+z^2=r^2\ .</math>
The sphere's radius has to be chosen such that the intersection with the ellipsoid is contained in two planes through the origin.
Multiplication of the ellipsoid's equation by <math>r^2</math> and subtracting the sphere's equation yields:
:<math>\left(\frac{r^2}{a^2}-1\right)\;x^2+\left(\frac{r^2}{b^2}-1\right)\;y^2+\left(\frac{r^2}{c^2}-1\right)\;z^2=0\ .</math>
This equation describes a pair of planes, if one of the 3 coefficients is zero. In case of  <math>\ r=a\ </math> or <math>\ r=c\ </math> the equation is only fulfilled by either the x-axis or the z-axis. Only in case of <math>\ r=b\ </math> one gets a pair of planes  with equation 
*<math>\left(\frac{b^2}{a^2}-1\right)\;x^2+\left(\frac{b^2}{c^2}-1\right)\;z^2=0\ \quad \leftrightarrow \quad z=\pm \tfrac{c}{a}\sqrt{\tfrac{a^2-b^2}{b^2-c^2}}\; x \ ,</math>
because only in this case the remaining coefficients have different signs (due to: <math>a>b>c</math>).

The diagram gives an impression of more common intersections between a sphere and an ellipsoid and highlights the exceptional circular case (blue).

If the values of the semi-axes are approaching, the two pencils of planes (and circles) approach either. For <math>a=b</math> all the planes are orthogonal to the z-axis (rotation axis).

{{math proof|title=Proof of property  (P)|
Turning the ellipsoid around  the y-axis such that one of the two circles (blue) lies in the x-y-plane results in a new equation of the ellipsoid:
:<math>Ax^2+By^2+Cz^2+D{\color{red}xz}=E</math>
For <math>z=0</math> one gets <math>Ax^2+By^2=E</math>, which has to be the equation of a circle. This is only true, if <math>A=B\ne 0,\ E>0</math>. 
The intersection of the ellipsoid by a plane with equation <math>z=z_0</math>, (parallel to the x-y-plane) has the equation
:<math>A(x^2+y^2)+Dz_0 x=E-Cz_0^2</math>.
This equation describes a ''circle'' or a point or the empty set. Center and radius of the circle can be found be [[completing the square]].}}

== Elliptical hyperboloid of one sheet==
[[File:Hyperboloid-1-KSE.svg|thumb|hyperboloid of one sheet]]
For  the [[hyperboloid]] of one sheet with equation 
: <math>\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}-\frac{z^2}{c^2}=1\ , \quad a>b\ , c>0 </math>
analogously one gets for the intersection with the sphere <math>\ x^2+y^2+z^2=r^2\ </math> the equation
:<math>\left(\frac{r^2}{a^2}-1\right)\;x^2+\left(\frac{r^2}{b^2}-1\right)\;y^2-\left(\frac{r^2}{c^2}+1\right)\;z^2=0\ .</math>
Only for <math>\ r=a\ </math> one gets a pair of planes:
:<math>\left(\frac{a^2}{b^2}-1\right)\;y^2-\left(\frac{a^2}{c^2}+1\right)\;z^2=0\ \quad
\leftrightarrow \quad z=\pm \frac{c}{b}\sqrt{\frac{a^2-b^2}{a^2+c^2}}\; y \ ,\ </math>

== Elliptical cylinder ==
[[File:Zylinder-KSE.svg|thumb|elliptical cylinder]]
For the elliptical [[cylinder]] with equation
: <math>\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1\ , \quad a>b\ ,</math>
one gets the equation
:<math>\left(\frac{r^2}{a^2}-1\right)\;x^2+\left(\frac{r^2}{b^2}-1\right)\;y^2-z^2=0\ .</math>
Only for <math>\ r=a\ </math> one gets a pair of planes:
:<math>\left(\frac{a^2}{b^2}-1\right)\;y^2-z^2=0\ \quad
\leftrightarrow \quad z=\pm \frac{\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}{b}\; y \ .\ </math>

== Elliptical paraboloid ==
[[File:Paraboloid-KSE.svg|thumb|elliptical paraboloid]]
For the elliptical [[paraboloid]] with equation
:<math>ax^2+by^2-z=0\ , \quad a{\color{red}{<}}b\ ,</math>
one chooses a sphere containing the vertex (origin) and with center on the axis (z-axis) :
:<math>x^2+y^2+(z-r)^2=r^2 \quad \leftrightarrow \quad x^2+y^2+z^2-2rz=0 \ . </math>
After elimination of the linear parts one gets the equation
:<math>(2ra-1)\;x^2+(2rb-1)\;y^2-z^2=0\ .</math>
Only for <math>r=\tfrac{1}{2a}</math> one gets a pair of planes :
:<math>\left(\frac{b}{a}-1\right)\; y^2-z^2=0  \quad
\leftrightarrow \quad z=\pm \sqrt{\frac{b-a}{a}}\; y \ .\ </math>

== Elliptical hyperboloid of two sheets==
[[File:Hyperboloid-2s-KSE.svg|thumb|elliptical hyperboloid of two sheets]]
The [[hyperboloid]] of two sheets with equation 
:<math>-\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} +\frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1 \ ,\quad a>b \ , \ c>0 \ ,</math>
is shifted at first such that one vertex is the origin (s. diagram):
:<math>-\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} +\frac{(z+c)^2}{c^2} = 1  \quad
\leftrightarrow \quad \ -\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} +\frac{z^2}{c^2} +\frac{2z}{c} = 0 \ .</math>
Analogously to the paraboloid case one chooses a sphere containing the origin with center on the z-axis:
:<math>x^2+y^2+(z-r)^2=r^2 \quad \leftrightarrow \quad x^2+y^2+z^2-2zr=0 \ . </math>
After elimination of the linear parts one gets the equation
:<math>\left(-\frac{r}{a^2}+\frac{1}{c}\right)\;x^2+\left(-\frac{r}{b^2}+\frac{1}{c}\right)\;y^2 +\left(\frac{r}{c^2}+\frac{1}{c}\right)z^2=0\ .</math>
Only for  <math>r=\tfrac{a^2}{c}</math> one gets a pair of planes:
:<math>\left(-\frac{a^2}{b^2c}+\frac{1}{c}\right)\;y^2+\left(\frac{a^2}{c^3}+\frac{1}{c}\right)\;z^2=0\ \quad
\leftrightarrow \quad z=\pm \frac{c}{b}\sqrt{\frac{a^2-b^2}{a^2+c^2}}\; y \ . </math>

== Elliptical cone ==
[[File:Kegel-KSE.svg|thumb|elliptical cone]]
The [[elliptical cone]] with equation 
:<math>\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} -z^2= 0 \ ,\quad a>b \ ,</math>
is shifted such that the vertex is ''not'' the origin (see diagram):
:<math>\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} -(z-1)^2= 0 \quad \leftrightarrow \quad \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} -z^2+2z= 1.</math>
Now a sphere with center at the origin is suitable:
:<math>x^2+y^2+z^2=r^2 \ . </math>
Elimination of <math>x^2</math> yields:
:<math>\left(\frac{a^2}{b^2}-1\right)\; y^2 -(1+a^2)\; z^2+2a^2z=a^2-r^2 \ .</math>
In this case completing the square gives:
:<math>\frac{a^2-b^2}{b^2}\; y^2-(1+a^2)\left(z-\frac{a^2}{1+a^2}\right)^2 = a^2-\frac{a^4}{1+a^2}-r^2 \ .</math>
In order to get the equation of a pair of planes, the right part of the equation has to be zero, which is true for <math>r=\tfrac{a}{\sqrt{1+a^2}}\ .</math>
The solution for z gives:
:<math>z=\frac{a^2}{1+a^2}\pm\frac{1}{b}\sqrt{\frac{a^2-b^2}{1+a^2}}\; y \ .</math>
